#1193. Harry Kane is 'still processing' his Ballon d'Or win, so he went back to the only thing he knows

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MUNICH – Less than an hour into a casual second-round cup match, a pocket of Bayern Munich fans in one corner of the Allianz Arena had moved on from reveling over Michael Olise's brace against second-division side Magdeburg. Their attention was instead on the group of substitutes who were warming up behind the opponent's goal and one person in particular.

It was a likely place for Harry Kane to spend a Wednesday evening, no matter the circumstances. Considering Bayern's relative strengths, the coaching staff had already hoped to give Kane the night off, especially with Borussia Dortmund awaiting this weekend and a trip to Atletico Madrid in the UEFA Champions League coming up on Tuesday. This was no ordinary midweek cup game, though, the pre-match guard of honor from his teammates as clear a sign as any of the occasion. It was Kane's first time back since winning the Ballon d'Or on Monday, doing so in his hometown of London.

The warm-ups were the only glimpse the crowd got of him on Wednesday, Bayern getting business done swiftly with a 6-1 win. Yet, Kane's appearance on the sidelines alone was celebratory, both after becoming the first Englishman to win the individual accolade in 25 years and the first player from the Bundesliga to do it since Matthias Sammer accomplished the feat in 1996. It was the type of thing that required an afterparty that allegedly stretched long after a delayed, bloated ceremony came to an end at around 11 p.m. local time, though Kane insisted he "didn't party too hard." It also allowed him to follow up a crowning achievement the only way he knows how – "straight back to work."

Kane trained on Tuesday and would have been ready to play if called upon on Wednesday, and is expected to prepare as usual for Saturday's clash with Dortmund. It comes as little surprise for a player who has rarely chased individual accolades. He has repeatedly insisted that his goal every four years is to win the World Cup with England, not the golden boot and left boyhood club Tottenham Hotspur for greater collective opportunities with Bayern in 2023 despite being just 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's Premier League goalscoring record at the age of 30. The spotlight has followed Kane for much of his career but he has always chosen to share it. There is no flexibility with the attention the Ballon d'Or carries, though; only one person can win it, no matter how team-oriented that person happens to be.

"It's strange," Kane said. "It's not my normal thing to enjoy. Even the guys, when I was walking out to warm up and they're all there clapping. I don't know. I get quite, maybe, embarrassed by it, but I know this is a big deal and I felt that obviously in the event, I felt that since with the reception and how much messages I've got from not just friends and family but people sending my number to other coaches and people just that have known me or know of me and they all wanted to just say well done. I think I'm still processing everything, to be honest, but look, I know it's a really big deal so I appreciate everyone, and you know, even on Saturday, I know we're going to do something before the game and all this, and it's important to do because it's a big celebration as well."

Even in his hometown on Monday, surrounded both by loved ones and his Bayern teammates who chanted his name in the London Palladium as Ronaldo revealed he had won the sport's ultimate individual prize, Kane felt out of place.

"A lot of nerves and just different emotions compared to a football match or anything like that and a lot of waiting around and just trying to picture what it'd be like if I did win but honestly, just really special," he said. "The support I've had from friends, family, fans, text messages, social media has just been overwhelming almost."

There is a lot Kane has not considered about life post-Ballon d'Or, either, like where the trophy might rest or what will come of the gold-flaked schnitzel that was made by a Bavarian restaurant and delivered to his home.

"I didn't actually eat it yesterday," he said. "With the match being today, I have a routine of what I eat and stuff but now, obviously, I appreciate it. It's a nice tradition that we have so to have a gold one, let's just keep them coming."

True to form, Kane has found the most comfort in a busy week in a return to his familiar routine.

"I think just being back to football," he said. "It feels like the Freiburg game [on Sunday] was six weeks ago. So much has happened in 48 hours. It was nice just to be back. A bit of normality, seeing the fans, getting a reception before the game, obviously, and then honestly just being back with the boys and just watching football and watching the boys play again so it's been a whirlwind of a 48 hours, and it's nice to just kind of be here and feel at home again."

He admitted he needs to add a new item to the routine at home, though – protecting the Ballon d'Or from his four children, aged nine to three.

"My wife and kids are still in London right now," he noted. "They get back on Friday so I haven't actually seen my kids since I won. I spoke to them, obviously, on FaceTime and stuff so I'm excited to see them and show them the trophy. I know they'll be trying to play with it and pick it up and it's quite heavy and so I might have to keep an eye on it this time but normally, the two boys, especially, just smash the ball around and then whoever wins picks up the trophy that I bring home but I'll have to explain it's a little bit more precious, so we'll have to keep an eye on it."

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1189. Inside Mohamed Salah's new life after his Liverpool fall-out: LEWIS STEELE visits Turkey's 30th biggest city, where the Egyptian King hikes, drinks salted yoghurt - and still gets hero worship

Published: 07:03 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 12:12 EDT, 6 November 2026

It started just minutes after touchdown in Turkey.

In a taxi journey across Istanbul's intercontinental bridge to Fenerbahce's stadium, the driver took a break from lighting up a cigarette or shouting profanities at other road users. He turned, looked me in the eye, and asked: 'You know Mohamed Salah?'

Two and a half hours after fighting through mind-blowing traffic (think your gridlocked motorway at 5pm multiplied by 100), on arrival at Liverpool's press conference, one gentleman did not even exchange pleasantries. He shoved a selfie stick in my face and asked about Salah.

And these two encounters were 650 miles away from where the Egyptian player now plies his trade. This fandom was only a starter when compared to the main course of Salahmania that greeted us upon arrival in the port city of Trabzon, to the east of Turkey on the coast of the Black Sea.

Here, his face and name were everywhere you looked. 'You come for Salah?' enquired the hotel receptionist. Upon hearing that was indeed the purpose of the visit, he upgraded the room to a superior suite overlooking the ocean. Result.

The streets of this city, which feels a world apart from the bustling metropolis of Istanbul, never mind Liverpool, are packed with antique dealers, and markets selling two-foot-long fish for less than £1 and the local delicacy of hamsi (anchovy to you and me).

Mohamed Salah can relax in Trabzon and has taken multiple hiking trips in the highlands (Source: Instagram/Mohamed Salah)

Fans have now taken to posing at the same spots Salah appeared at - such is their hero worship

Everywhere you turned, there was a nod to Salah. His name was heard in conversations as the melodic call to prayer rang out from the nearby Hagia Sophia mosque, his picture seemed to be hung from every building and his name was on the back of every shirt being sported in town.

Shops were selling mugs, scarves, plates, masks and even cigarette lighters shaped like Salah.

At the futuristic waterfront stadium known as Papara Park, Salahmania continued - with punters putting on impromptu barbecues and DJ sets from beside their cars similar to tailgates in American sports. Everyone in this city was dancing to the beat of the Egyptian King.

Fans, many in Trabzonspor-coloured jester hats with bells on, glowed about Salah. Most do not speak a word of English in this city not far from the Armenian and Georgian border. But those who could summed up the mood.

'We love him, he is going to make us champions,' said one.

Another told us: 'People across the country now support Trabzonspor and people come from other countries, people want us to win just because of Mohamed Salah.'

Trabzonspor supporters told Daily Mail Sport: 'We love him, he is going to make us champions'

Everywhere you turned there was a nod to Salah in his new club's kit

There were plenty of children in the crowd, and more women than expected. Some had come from afar to see him, others could not believe that Salah had chosen their team and hometown.

So, why Trabzon? Why did Salah choose this project in Turkey's 30th biggest city? Why not one of the three Istanbul giants – Fenerbahce, Galatasaray or Besiktas – who have won 28, 27 and 21 Turkish titles respectively, compared to Trabzonspor's seven, including only one since 1984.

The answers are obvious, according to sources. Salah, now 34, wanted a place where he could enjoy his football without the intense scrutiny. Every word and facial expression would generate days of news coverage in Liverpool or Istanbul or another one of Europe's giant cities.

On the outskirts of Trabzon, Salah can relax, hiking up to a group of boulders in Yayla. Even there, he's worshipped, though. Trabzonspor fans flock there to pose for photographs on the same rock where he sat for a photo posted on his Instagram.

Salah's family are settled, he is becoming obsessed with chess and he has started drinking the Turkish salted-yoghurt drink ayran each day.

On the pitch, there is a belief Trabzonspor can beat the big three and end Galatasaray's four-year grip on the title.

The team also stars former Liverpool midfielder Fabinho and ex-Manchester United goalkeeper Andre Onana, while Jerome Boateng, once a stalwart at Bayern Munich, is assistant manager. Boss Thomas Reis was poached from Ludogorets and has lost just once since his arrival.

Salah is settled with his family and faces less scrutiny than in Istanbul or Liverpool (Source: Instagram/Mohamed Salah)

Salah has scored 10 goals and assisted five more in his 15 games in Turkey so far

The highlight so far came on September 19, when Salah scored a hat-trick in a 4-0 thumping of Galatasaray. Trabzonspor have won seven league games in a row and will aim to go deep in the Conference League despite Thursday's undeserved 1-0 defeat to Freiburg.

Salah has scored 10 goals and assisted in five more in his 15 games in Turkey.

'Everyone wants to work with a star the size of Mohamed Salah,' striker Paul Onuachu, once of Southampton, told us after that game. 'He is a top guy and a world star.

'He adds so much to us and helps all of us, thanks to his experience and quality, and he contributes positively to the development of our team.

'I am grateful for him. It is a blessing to play with him.'

Salah did not have the rub of the green in the clash with the German side, who were Europa League finalists last year. But a trip to Papara Park underlined an answer to those wondering just why he picked Trabzon and not any of his other mega-money offers.

A man wearing Trabzonspor's claret and light blue colours shows off his support for Salah

A trip to Papara Park underlined an answer to those wondering just why he picked Trabzon

He had approaches from America, and the Saudi Arabian federation tried to sign him right until the day he jetted into Trabzon - where he was greeted by 35,000 fans with fireworks and flares. Besiktas held advanced talks with Salah's agent Ramy Abbas.

But Trabzonspor won the race and Salah is playing with a smile again, even though that face pulled a bit of a grimace when he spotted a familiar face or two from the English press pack waiting for him after the game.

His laugh faded into an expression that said: 'I thought I got rid of you lot pestering me!'

That face confirmed his reason for joining Trabzonspor: Salah is out of the spotlight – certainly while still in with a chance to win trophies and maintain a good level of football until next summer's Africa Cup of Nations.

After a public fall-out with Liverpool that saw the final year of his contract ripped up and him accuse the Anfield club of 'throwing him under the bus', it feels like Salah is feeling at home and happy again.

It's not difficult to turn down the multiple opportunities to buy Salah-branded magnets or shirts or teddies or socks or lighters as we bid farewell to Trabzon, but it is hard to escape the conclusion that the feeling of love is mutual in this football-mad city.

#1187. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Paz was just unplayable for much of an evening when United never got close to getting to grips with the young Argentine, whose big physique belies a bewitching ability on the ball. Jacobo Ramón completed the rout before Joshua Zirkzee scored the most hollow of goals for United late on.

United, by contrast, were a sorry collection of strangers. It was impossible to discern a game plan. United were sent out in a strange 4-2-4, with Fernandes and Youri Tielemans operating as almost double false nines. Glenn Hoddle said on TNT Sports that it was like United were “playing in chains”.

Neither looked sure of what they were supposed to be doing. There was just a giant hole where the attack should have been. Everything about them was slow, leaden. The confusion was contagious. Everywhere you looked there were players second-guessing themselves, uncertain of their role and position and habitually a yard or two or three off the pace. But was there any excuse for not running, for so little effort?

The space Paz was afforded to curl in a fine finish less than two minutes in was alarming in the extreme. Carrick brought on Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo for the lamentable Mateus Cunha and Andrey Santos at half-time, but United just got worse.

There was not so much as a snip at the heels of the same player when Paz ghosted in from the right flank, running 30 yards deep into the penalty area before again finishing coolly for the third. Ramón had a free header for the fourth.

United enjoy a spell inside the attacking third to close the half, but it’s too late, at least for the first 45 minutes. The referee blows his whistle and we reach half-time with Como a goal to the good.

There are boos at half-time from United’s travelling support.

United send both of their full-backs forward and it gives Cunha the space to get a shot away from just outside of the box, but his curled effort sails over.

There will be one minute of time added on at the end of this half.

That’s a let off for United. Yan Couto, one of two former Manchester City signings in the Como team, carves open the United defence with a lovely pass and Douvikas should have done better with the finish.

Amazing the difference when you have a centre forward prepared to run in behind. Who would have thought it?

Baturina is the latest to threaten Lammens’ goal. His strike from the edge of the box stings the Belgian’s gloves and Douvikas, who attempts to latch on to the rebound, is offside.

Penalty shout for Como! Douvikas is sent through and it looks as though Lammens is in trouble as he sticks out a leg over which the Greek tumbles, but replays show Lammens withdraws his outstretched limb in the nick of time.

There was also an offside in the build-up, so it does not matter anyway.

Milla and Perrone are really pulling the strings in Como’s midfield. The former comes from the Jose Bordalas/Getafe school of football (think Tony Pulis during peak Britannia era) but you would not guess it given the way he manipulates the ball.

This game has entered into something of a holding pattern, with Como retaining possession as United chase shadows, desperately trying to lock off the centre of the park.

Here, Coute inverts, picking up the ball in the inside right channels before spinning in a ball over the top for Douvikas to stride on to, but the Greece forward shanks his shot over the bar.

Thirty four minutes in and the first chants of “attack, attack, attack” can be heard from the United fans. There is currently a giant hole where you would expect United’s strikers to be. It’s so poor.

Lammens does well to get down smartly and keep out a Douvikas effort, speared towards the near post after a sweeping counter attack. The resulting corner fails to threaten United’s defensive unit.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

The detail on United’s passes has been so poor thus far, with Como picking up loose balls all over the pitch.

Penalty shout for Como! Da Cunha, Douvikas and Baturina combine expertly through the middle, trading the ball with cultured one-touch passes. Baturina is felled by Maguire inside United’s box just as he was gearing up to shoot, but neither the referee nor the VAR are minded to intervene. There is a touch, but it does seem very slight.

United have gone with the box midfield once more, with Fernandes rolling inside as a false 9. Como are counteracting United’s movements through Paz dropping in, so Carrick’s men are struggling to take control of the central zones.

Mbeumo bursts towards the by-line but Ramon gets back sharply to divert the ball behind for a corner, which is easily dealt with.

United drop into a deep block, forcing Como to build around the outside. The ball is worked to the adventurous Couto who loses his boot after an overzealous challenge from Cunha and he earns a free-kick for his troubles, but Da Cunha’s delivery fails to beat the first man.

Chance! Da Cunha plays a lovely through-ball into the right channel for Paz to gallop on to and he flashes the ball across the face of goal, but Maguire gets there before Douvikas and the ball is cleared.

United are struggling to string passes together as Paz cuts out a Lammens pass out from the back, but he cannot keep the ball in play.

United need to settle, and here they decide it best to keep hold of the ball for a while. There are a few sideways passes but the ball goes back to Como.

Valle makes a burst down the left and Dalot’s contact results in a foul, but the free-kick is not up to much.

Como 1 Manchester United 0 (Paz) Well, we said he was special! Como work the ball out to the right, with Da Cunha picking out Paz on the edge of the box. Neither of United’s centre-halves are minded to close the Argentine down, and he opens up his body before shaping the ball around Lammens and inside the far post. Golazo.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is important.”

Andrey Santos, one of United’s summer signings, was asked for his thoughts on Lisandro Martínez’s explosive interview in which he took aim at the club’s hierarchy for their strategy in the latest transfer window. The Brazilian said: “We know the comments [of] Licha, but I think now it’s done so we have to move on and focus on tomorrow [Wednesday].

When pressed on whether Martínez had addressed the squad about his remarks, Santos added: “No, no, no. Nothing happened, as you know we are on the same page, so we believe in ourselves, in your team-mates, your coach, your staff, so I think this is the most important.”

Jack Fletcher and Tynan Thompson played for United against Como in the Uefa Youth League earlier in the day and the pair are named among the substitutes. Fletcher played for 71 minutes, and scored, and Thompson the whole game, which United lost 2-1.

It’s happened before where players have played in the Youth League then made the senior bench later in the day although the very youthful bench is a reflection of just how many absentees Carrick has at the moment.

We’d been braced for thunder and lightning and torrential rain in Como today but so far at least the weather has been pretty kind. It’s raining and moody but far from the severe weather warnings forecast. Michael Carrick will hope that is a portent - the start of a clearing of the storm that has engulfed the club this season.

The United manager is missing nine players through injury, illness and suspension so Matthijs de Ligt gets his first outing for 11 months following a serious back injury. Carlos Baleba has dropped to the bench - he’s still working his way back to full fitness after a long spell out himself - so Mason Mount comes into midfield and Amad Diallo makes way for Matheus Cunha.

Cesc Fabregas has done a fine job at Como and will hope to further enhance that burgeoning reputation with an historic win. United desperately need results - it’s two wins in 10 in all competitions - and face Bournemouth on Sunday after this.

I wonder whether Zirkzee is having flashbacks to a certain team-talk delivered by Vincent Kompany...

The last time De Ligt played for Manchester United, Ruben Amorim was still at the helm. A lot has changed since then (or has it?!) and this evening will be the Dutch defender’s first taste of first-team action under Michael Carrick.

There is no place in Fabregas’ starting XI for Robert Sanchez, who is on loan from Chelsea and conceded three against Feyenoord in the last round of Champions League matches.

Emerging talent Nico Paz will be one to watch out for.

Starting XI: Butez; Couto, Ramon, Kempf, Valle; Perrone, Da Cunha, Milla; Paz, Baturina; Douvikas

Substitutes: Ginelli, Sanchez, Smolcic, Kaiki, Dossena, Caqueret, Ricci, Liberali

Starting XI to face Manchester United. 📋 #ComoManUtd #UCL https://t.co/76psp5qBVl

De Ligt comes into the starting XI for his appearance since November 2025 (325 days ago) as Carrick makes four changes to the side which drew at Leeds United.

Lining up for United this evening... ✨ #UCL https://t.co/nyKC4GpWgH

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of Manchester United’s trip to Como in the Champions League. Under normal circumstances, a visit to the idyllic Lombardy city would be a source of thrill and wonder, but Michael Carrick heads into the eye of a literal and proverbial storm at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia with his team desperately hoping to reverse their fortunes.

Absolutely tipping it down in Como, with 64mm of rain forecast before #MUFC kick-off here tomorrow ☔️ https://t.co/WvI3X8dilh

Two wins – against Ipswich Town and Sabah – in United’s first 10 matches of the season, a public outburst from Lisandro Martínez and accusations of a “toxic culture” at the club have piled pressure on Carrick. And an uninspiring draw at Elland Road on Sunday did little to settle the rising tide of discontent within the United fanbase.

When asked for his team news, the first words that came from the United head coach’s mouth were: “Right, bit of mixed bag to be honest.” That was not a great sign, and Carrick will be without Martínez, Kobbie Mainoo, Luke Shaw, Ayden Heaven, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu, who are injured, while Leny Yoro serves a suspension following his red card against Atlético Madrid.

Like United, the hosts are without a handful of key players, with Moise Kean, Trevoh Chalobah, Assane Diao and Jesus Rodriguez missing from the match-day squad. The abundantly talented Argentine No 10 Nico Paz will feature, however, and he will be keen to showcase his talents in the Champions League.

Como have ascended from Serie B to Europe’s top table in three seasons (and from bankruptcy in nine) under Cesc Fàbregas’ watchful eye. The Spaniard is a minority owner and shareholder of the club, but as head coach he has introduced an incisive, possession-based style of play which contains hints of the managerial greats under whom he played: Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho, Vicente del Bosque, Antonio Conte etc.

#1186. A death sentence for ‘sloppy’ cancers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Lorenzo Valcanover is in the Division of Oncogenomics, Oncode Institute, the Netherlands Cancer Institute, Amsterdam 1066 CX, the Netherlands.

Reuven Agami is in the Division of Oncogenomics, Oncode Institute, the Netherlands Cancer Institute, Amsterdam 1066 CX, the Netherlands, and the Department of Genetics, Erasmus University Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

Identifying cellular properties that distinguish a cancer from healthy tissue is a crucial step for developing efficient treatments. One such characteristic is the ‘sloppy’ way in which some cancer cells implement translation — the process by which proteins are made from messenger RNA by protein complexes called ribosomes. This process can go awry. Writing in Nature, Wang et al.1 reveal a cancer-specific mechanism by which translation loses its normal ‘track’ of how it reads an mRNA sequence to encode the expected amino acids, resulting in a phenomenon called frameshifting. This generates proteins that have a distinct sequence of amino acids that are not usually made, and the authors show that this abnormality might be exploited for therapeutic purposes.

#1184. From last place to the playoffs: How the Philadelphia Union pulled off MLS's most stunning turnaround

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

CHESTER, Pa. -- At the end of the World Cup, the Philadelphia Union were at the bottom of the Eastern Conference and all of Major League Soccer with only seven points, moving on from Supporters' Shield-winning head coach Bradley Carnell and turning to 36-year-old Ryan Richter to save the season. Given Richter's path as someone who oversaw the Union's MLS Next Pro side before becoming an assistant under Jim Curtin with the first team, it seemed like a moment where the Union would be in the process of preparing for next season and seeing what they did next.

But with the return of a familiar face in Kai Wagner, a meeting at Two Persons Coffee in South Philadelphia between captain Alejandro Bedoya and Richter, and one of the most impressive runs that we've seen of youth talent in league history, the Union were able to clinch a place in the MLS Cup playoffs, and they did it in impressive fashion, too, by playing Nashville SC to a scoreless draw away from home without 17-year-old phenom Cavan Sullivan being available for the match. It caps off a turnaround that has seen the Union pick up 40 points since the World Cup, winning 12 matches, drawing four, and only losing one. Those 40 points outpace the second-best team in the time range, which is Nashville SC, by five.

Sullivan has been one of the spark plugs of this improvement with seven goals and 11 assists, with most of that coming after the World Cup break, but with 38 of the Union's 59 league goals absent for that game as Bruno Damiani and Milan Iloski missed out on the match, it truly showed the mentality that the squad has.

Plenty preach about "next-man-up" mentality, but matches like this one show why no one should want to face the Union in the playoffs. If the season ended today, they'd face Inter Miami in a three-game series, which would be sure to bring fireworks after the scuffle that their last meeting created, but there's still more work to do with two games remaining, as the Union could slide down to the eight-versus-nine play-in game if they lose their final two games of the regular season.

Under Carnell, the Union were a traditional high-press team that tried to force their opponents into mistakes. While it worked with only MLS games to play, adding in the Concacaf Champions Cup saw the team unable to keep up that intensity, especially without Wagner at left back and with Neil Pierre on loan in Denmark instead of being with the squad. While Richter did benefit from both of these players being in the mix, he has also dialed things back to more of a zonal press, allowing the midfield to have time to rest in between plays so that they can keep the same intensity at minute 90 as they have entering the game.

Pierre and Nathan Harriel on the back line have assisted greatly with that, being mobile centerbacks in their own right. Richter knows the impact of having a 6-foot-7 defender like Pierre, who is also comfortable when being on an island, and it's clear how he helps the attack function.

"We can be super aggressive because Neil is comfortable in one-on-one situations. If it's a direct ball, he wins; he eats all of these. If it's open space that he has to defend, physically, he can deal with that, and he's also a good defender," Richter said. "The way he puts out so many fires allows us to be aggressive higher up the field, because we know when they play the ball long that we have someone who cleans this up almost every time."

Putting that in front of three-time MLS Goalkeeper of the Year Andre Blake, it's easy to see why the Union's defense has improved from the first half of the season, but the attack is where major strides have been made.

You'd have to be living under a rock to have not heard the name Cavan Sullivan by now, and for good reason, as the 17-year-old has been taking MLS by storm and helping push the Union attack forward with his creativity. Since the World Cup break, Sullivan is second only to Evander in assists with nine and has pitched in goals alongside that. He may not be the biggest or fastest player on the pitch, but the quick bursts that he has into space have been tormenting defenses.

Alongside Pierre and Frankie Westfield, he was able to earn his first national team cap under Mauricio Pochettino and also didn't look out of place there either, but when speaking to him and people around the team, the shift in mentality is clear. Sullivan asked to do extra training during the World Cup break instead of taking the time off, and has come back a more complete player. Already set to join Manchester City when he turns 18 next year, the path for future development is clear (assuming City are in the Premier League), but this is one of the best American soccer prospects ever developed. Being able to play alongside his older brother Quinn also helps with this transition, but Cavan has grown into a player of his own, and while this season has been a coming-out party for him in many ways, the playoffs are going to be a moment that can thrust him into the stratosphere as he looks to lead his hometown club to the first MLS Cup title in their history.

Which American has the most goals in Major League Soccer? Usually, the answer to that question is Brian White, but this season, it also resides in Philadelphia in Milan Iloski, a longtime journeyman, he has found a home in Philadelphia and has scored 19 goals with seven assists, which is third in the league. After moving Tai Baribo to D.C. United, there were valid questions of where the Union's goals would come from, and Iloski has delivered and shown that there isn't a finish that he doesn't have in his locker, and he's not overperforming, either, with an xG of 18.77.

Alongside him, Bruno Damiani has stepped up with 12 goals, and the Uruguayan could be key to any serious playoff run that the team has. If teams crowd Sullivan and Iloski, other people on the team need to be able to make them pay, and Damiani is chief among them. The hope was that new signing Ezekiel Alladoh would be able to take on that mantle, but with one goal and one assist in 26 appearances, he may find minutes hard to come by in the playoffs unless there's an injury. While it's unlikely that they'd upset the likes of Nashville and Miami to win the MLS Cup, the mantra of "Why not us" has always carried Philadelphia and looking at these numbers, you can't say that they don't have a chance. Given that, it is also only a matter of time until the interim tag is removed from Richter's coaching title, but that's an offseason issue to deal with; right now, there are more soccer games to win.

#1182. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

#1180. Djed Spence opens up on becoming England's first-ever Muslim footballer

Djed Spenceâs call-up to Thomas Tuchelâs England squad for Septemberâs World Cup qualifiers was a career highlight in itself â but it also carried huge significance far beyond the pitch.

By earning his place in the squad, the Tottenham Hotspur defender has become the first openly practicing Muslim footballer to receive a senior England menâs call-up. Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Arsenal: The Inside Story of Arsenal’s Rebirth Under Mikel Arteta (Pan Macmillan, RRP £22).

This is a proper heavyweight clash but, sadly for the neutrals watching, Bayern are missing some big players. Michael Olise is suspended, Jamal Musiala is injured and Joshua Kimmich is unavailable following the death of his father.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Ice cold from Martinelli 🥶 https://t.co/uQEHb4x7eH

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1176. Epileptic seizures nearly vanish after people receive experimental gene therapy in their brains

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

A scan shows the brain of a man with epilepsy. A newly developed gene therapy targets locations in the brain that are the root of epileptic seizures. Credit: Allison Robbert/The Washington Post/Getty

Three people with epilepsy resistant to drug treatment saw the number of seizures they had per month fall by more than 90% after gene-laden viruses were infused directly into their brains as part of an early-stage clinical trial1.

In each participant, the gene therapy was precisely targeted to a small patch of brain tissue that was the source of their seizures. The viruses carried a gene that makes neurons sensitive to a specific drug, which works like a dimmer switch for the therapy. By combining gene therapy with a drug — an approach known as chemogenetics — researchers can adjust a treatment’s potency, which is not possible with other types of gene therapy. The trial participants did not experience serious side effects.

Genetic therapies offer new hope against incurable brain diseases

Genetic therapies offer new hope against incurable brain diseases

The results were reported today in The New England Journal of Medicine by Yang Dai, a neurosurgeon at Xuanwu Hospital of Capital Medical University in Beijing, and his colleagues. “It’s exciting that there’s such a dramatic effect, and that they see very few side effects,” says Matthew Walker, a neurologist at University College London, who was not associated with the study.

But Walker cautions that the study is small. He is also concerned about the long-term use of the drug that participants took after receiving the gene therapy. High doses of the drug, an anti-psychotic called clozapine, have been associated with cardiovascular problems and other negative effects. “In the future, hopefully there are going to be better drugs” for this form of treatment, says Walker, who is the co-founder of the start-up company Focalis Bio in Canterbury, UK, which is also developing gene therapies for epilepsy.

The three trial participants were adults with a common form of epilepsy caused by hippocampal sclerosis, a type of scarring in a region of the brain called the hippocampus. The participants had this scarring on only one side of the hippocampus. All three had been diagnosed with epilepsy 10–25 years earlier and had developed resistance to at least two anti-seizure drugs. They also had at least two seizure episodes per month, on average, over the three months before they enrolled in the trial.

The experimental treatment uses a virus called adeno-associated virus 9 to deliver a gene to neurons in the affected area. The gene was engineered to produce proteins specifically in excitatory cells — the ones that are involved in seizures.

Brain editing now ‘closer to reality’: the gene-altering tools tackling deadly disorders

Brain editing now ‘closer to reality’: the gene-altering tools tackling deadly disorders

The gene instructs neurons to produce a receptor that binds to clozapine. Clozapine acts like a switch and activates these receptors, reducing the activity of the targeted neurons, the authors say. That reduced activity helps to suppress the abnormal electrical activity that triggers seizures.

Two weeks after receiving the gene therapy during surgery, participants began taking a low dose of clozapine every eight hours. Around two months later, the average number of seizures per month had dropped from 4.5 to 0.5 for two of the participants and from 4 to 0 for the third. Because the study design focused on safety, rather than measuring efficacy, there was no control group.

Walker says that there might be other explanations for the improvement. He adds that it is also not clear whether the effect was because of the combination of gene therapy and clozapine or from one of those components alone.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03566-2

Dai, Y. et al. N. Engl. J. Med. 395, 1867–1869 (2026).

#1175. Inter and AC Milan unveil plans for new 71,500-seat Generali Stadium to replace iconic San Siro

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It was an historic day in Milan as Inter and AC Milan have finally unveiled the project for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, the current arena that hosts the home games of both teams. The new San Siro will be named "Generali Stadium" after the Italian insurance company Generali acquired the naming rights of the stadium in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years, according to multiple reports. The Generali Stadium will be ready by the 2031-2032 season, according to the two clubs, just in time for the UEFA 2032 Euro that will be co-hosted by Italy and Turkiye, with construction starting in 2028. The current San Siro will be demolished only after the new stadium is ready to be used by the teams, giving more time for fans to attend a match in the iconic Italian stadium that was built in 1926.

Let's now go into the details of the new arena: According to the joint news release from both clubs, it will be a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience". A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. A "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, AC Milan and Inter ownerships, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football".

Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the iconic Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a striking structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

Engineered to capture and intensify crowd energy, the stadium's acoustic design ensures supporters remain at the heart of the spectacle, helping create an environment designed to be among the most atmospheric in world football. Enhanced accessibility, modern hospitality concepts and a broad range of seating options, from world-class premium experiences to popular seating areas, will ensure the venue welcomes every generation of fan, while offering new ways to experience the game.

The two teams will continue to share their home stadium, a unique tradition that started in the late '40's of the 20th century, when Inter moved to San Siro as well. Unlike most of the teams around the world of soccer, Inter and AC Milan decided to continue sharing their home stadium after leaving the current arena. After years of failed projects and attempts, the new stadium is now a concrete reality. In 2025, the Milan City Council approved the sale of the city's San Siro stadium to the two clubs Inter and AC Milan. Now, the two Italian teams have decided to move into a new direction and era.

As Italian soccer is facing a crisis also regarding their infrastructures, the Generali Stadium can drastically increase the match revenues of both Inter and AC Milan, putting them at the level of the European rivals. At the same time, seeing the teams leave the legendary San Siro will be hard.

San Siro has been the home of AC Milan and Inter, but its history extends far beyond soccer. The iconic stadium has hosted some of the most memorable sporting and cultural events, including the opening ceremony of the 2026 Winter Olympic Games and legendary concerts by some of the biggest names in music. From Bob Marley's historic performance in 1980, the first-ever concert at San Siro, to unforgettable shows by the Rolling Stones, David Bowie, Michael Jackson, Madonna, Taylor Swift, U2 or Bruce Springsteen, who has famously described San Siro as his second home, the stadium has become a landmark far beyond the world of sport. Now, a new era is about to start but the "old" San Siro won't be forgotten.

Published: 12:34 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 14:16 EDT, 6 November 2026

Jack Grealish will return to Everton training after being dropped and exiled by David Moyes.

The 31-year-old was axed for back-to-back matches against Newcastle following a 'breach of club discipline' and is not part of the Toffees' matchday squad for the third game on the spin when they host Coventry tonight.

Grealish, who has made seven appearances since re-joining Everton for a second season-long loan spell from Man City in the summer, had been banished since failing to show up for a training session on Monday last week. It is understood staff struggled to make contact with the winger.

Grealish will now be reintegrated on a tailored training programme to regain match fitness and could be included in first-team sessions during the international break from next week.

Grealish had made four successive starts before he missed Everton's 2-0 defeat by Arsenal on October 24 due to illness.

Grealish was reported to have had back-to-back nights out prior to the Toffees' defeat in north London.

Jack Grealish, previously pictured out with a friend, was exiled by Everton but is now set to return to training with the team

David Moyes could start Grealish against Brentford after the international break

The three-time Premier League winner attended the Pride of Britain awards at the Grosvenor House hotel in London on October 19 where he presented the Child of Courage award to 12-year-old Zac Howells.

He is then reported to have finished the night of celebration off at Bam Karaoke Box, a karaoke hotspot in Victoria, central London.

According to the Sun, he stayed up until the early hours of the morning singing with his friends and enjoying the drinks on offer.

The next day, Grealish is believed to have returned to Cheshire, where he and many of his footballer friends live, to meet team-mates Jordan Pickford and Tyler Dibling at The Mauldeth pub in Wilmslow.

The trio, joined by Grealish's former City team-mate and captain Kyle Walker, where they watched Paris Saint-Germain's thrilling Champions League victory over Barcelona. A witness claimed to the Sun that they enjoyed a few drinks.

Moyes had been coy on the situation when asked about it on Thursday. He said: 'You probably know I'm not going to give any details, it is a club decision and I support that decision (for him to be punished). It is something I don't want to speak too much about.

'The one thing about Everton is that we have got really good values behind it. All the players stand up to the values and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch. From that point of view, I think the players did a brilliant job.'

Without Grealish once again, Everton are seeking to secure a third win in a row when they come up against former Toffees boss Frank Lampard and his Coventry team.

Grealish is reported to have gone on consecutive nights out after attending the Pride of Britain Awards on October 19

After the Coventry clash, Everton are next in Premier League action at Gtech Community Stadium against Brentford on November 23.

Grealish will be targeting a return in that fixture and hope he can begin to rebuild his relationship with Moyes over the next three weeks.

He has played for England 39 times and turned out for Everton on 22 occasions, scoring twice and providing six assists, with a nasty foot injury cut short his campaign last term.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

On Saturday, AC Milan will host Inter at San Siro for the first Derby della Madonnina of the season. It's a clash between two of the most important teams in Europe and the first derby for Portuguese coach Ruben Amorim, who joined AC Milan in the summer after leaving Manchester United in January. The two clubs will play at the iconic Italian arena, but on Thursday they unveiled plans for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, which both clubs currently share. The new San Siro will be named Generali Stadium after Italian insurer Generali acquired the naming rights in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years.

The project is a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience," according to the clubs. A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. The stadium is a "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, the owners of AC Milan and Inter, respectively, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football." Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a distinctive structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

#1167. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

#1163. ‘Tactical genius’ Emery outsmarts Maresca as City crash to first league defeat

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

On his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

City’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

What a strike from Nicolas Jackson to beat Gianluigi Donnarumma 😲 Villa Park erupts 🔊 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/zkuDVMevKF

Maresca said: “I’m not worried about Marc at all, he is playing every game since the season started for us and the national team so it’s not easy. He is ok, it [taking him off] was just a technical decision and like in all games managers make changes. He was on a yellow card and sometimes one yellow card can be dangerous.”

When asked if the goals were avoidable, Maresca said: “Absolutely, both. Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances. We will try again to win at Villa next season. I don’t think we deserved to lose but we learn from that and move on. You can always learn something. For sure there are things we can do better today.”

While much of the focus will be on City’s 100 per cent start to the league coming to an end, Emery got everything right here. From his team selection to his set-up and substitutions, he outsmarted Maresca on many levels. After the game, Villa defender Matty Cash described his manager as “a tactical genius”.

It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

Emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

For a long time, football has a system where you can tell who deserved to win or not. It is the scoreboard. For decades, longer even, you could tell who was the better team by looking at who had the most goals.

However, football managers persist with the idea that there is another ineffable reason that decides who deserves what. Enzo Maresca is apparently no different.

He told the BBC: “When we scored I had the feeling that we were in control and really for the entire game. We created many chances but unfortunately didn’t score them. We conceded one transition in the second half and they were very efficient because they scored. Bit unlucky and we learn from that.

“I was not here in the past but today I think we deserved something more.”

Here are his similar thoughts on TNT Sports.
